[AussieGargain] This is a fair question: this is from Google AI - If an Australian butcher or distributor wants to boast about real consumer eating quality, they will use the MSA (Meat Standards Australia) system. This system was built by testing real consumers and scores meat by specific cut and cooking methods:
MSA 3-Star: Good everyday quality.
MSA 4-Star: Premium quality.
MSA 5-Star: Supreme quality.
AUS-MEAT Marbling Score (MS): Ranked from 0 to 9+ (standard for high-end grain-fed or Wagyu).
[jv] This is a fair question
A question the Rep has avoided answering…
[F2F] MSA only scores the level of intramuscular fat. It has nothing at all to do with eating quality.
The score for the entire cow is determined using a single image off the scotch fillet when the cow carcass is cut in half.
It's one of the most disconnected and useless ratings scale I've ever come across.
Both the abattoir and farmers must pay a large annual fee to get their meat "graded" against highly subjective colour and marbling measures.
Is this meat graded.. no.
Would I personally pay more for graded meat.. absolutely not.

[Satchimo] I'm not sure that is as logical as it sounds.
Wagyu has intramuscular fat marbling whereas you are comparing this with regular beef and just adding a bit of extra random visceral fat to balance the meat to fat ratios. It's basically two completely different products.
This means that the Wagyu melts from the inside (at a much lower temperature) whereas the "add some extra visceral fat" method melts from the outside and will coat the meat granules in that waxy, coat the roof of your mouth texture instead of being incorporated into the muscle.
Then there's the whole taste difference, including whether the "special blend" is produced from grain or grass fed cattle.
As the melting points differ so much, I daresay that two different chemical reactions are involved as well which will also affect taste and texture outcomes.
Idk, I have no skin in Wagyu game, but all cows aren't equal and just like potatoes and apples (for example), different varieties do produce different tastes, textures and outcomes.
[Cheaplikethebird] @Satchimo: Yeah I don't think it's going to make that much of a difference after a couple passes through the grinder. I'm also aware of the lower melting point but again not sure it'd make much of a difference in most things you'd be using mince for.
I grind burgers weekly, haven't noticed much of a difference when I supplement with my porterhouse fat trimmings. I do two passes through a coarse plate.
[Satchimo] @Cheaplikethebird: You are more than likely correct. I have very minimal experience with Wagyu and I can honestly say that it had never even crossed my mind that somebody would use it for mince.
[F2F] @Satchimo: No cow is just steaks and roasts. You’ll always get trim to mince.
[Satchimo] @F2F: At $50 per kg, I'm going to be using that trim for stir fry, stroganoff or cube/stew type cuts, I don't want to be selling very much of it in mince!
[Tythefly86] @Satchimo: Isn't visceral fat only the fat around the organs? Most people aren't eating organs these days and I didn't see you mention liver. Most people eat cow muscle and I thought a lot of the fat on steaks is just the outer coat between the skin and the muscles right?
[Satchimo] @Tythefly86: Yes, but the other fat sources are mostly still attached to the steaks that you're selling. I envisaged that Cheap was referring to the fat that wasn't otherwise used/sold. If I sell the fat in mince, I can get a max of $25 a kg. If I sell that fat still attached to a rump, or rib fillet etc, I get to sell it for substantially more…
It would be weird to cut the fat off your sirloin or rump only to mince it.
Why did I need to mention liver? People are still buying offal. We do only stock tripe for special orders, but we have to source extra caul and intestines as we use more than we can produce.
We buy in all our lamb (pork, chicken/poultry & game too) and buy kidney, intestine, brains, liver, heart. Pork intestine. Chicken livers & hearts. We use as much natural sausage casings as we can get our hands on, otherwise we have to use synthetic ones to make up the shortfall.
Always include a good helping of offal in pet's mince as well. It's nice and healthy/nutrient dense, particularly for those relying on a raw food nutritional plan, but apart from being super tasty, it makes it a much richer colour for the humans buying the pet food :)
[myisk] Wagyu fat does taste different to regular beef fat. It doesn't leave a fatty waxy feeling in your mouth because of the lower melting temp of Wagyu fat. So a Wagyu mince with 20% fat would be more enjoyable than a regular beef mince with 20% fat.
This deal doesn't say what marble grade the meat is so it's a bit of a gamble. And "Full Wagyu" is a bit ambiguous. Wagyu with 100% of genetics that can be traced back to Japan is called fullblood, so is that what they mean? Or do they just mean all the meat in this box is considered to be Wagyu including Wagyu crosses? But even fullblood Wagyu marbling can differ a lot due to the particular animal's genetics and what they are fed. I'm surprised this is grass fed and finished because Wagyu are normally at least grain finished because it's a lot harder to get higher marbling with just grass.
